tldr: By restricting the massive VLA model to moments of object contact and delegating free-space motion to a fast classical motion planner, task completion is sped up by up to 2.5x and energy consumption is cut in half without sacrificing success rates.
hero_caption: SkipVLA in action during pick-and-place with a physical 6-DoF arm. Free-space motion (the white arrows in ① and movement from ② to ③) is handled rapidly by a classical planner, while control switches to the VLA only during delicate contact skills like grasping and placing (red ② and yellow ③).
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map camera images and natural language instructions directly to robot actions, attracting widespread attention for their generalist capabilities. However, running inference on multi-billion-parameter networks in every control loop introduces massive latency. This leads to sluggish task execution and causes power consumption to spike on edge devices, posing a serious practical bottleneck.

The authors observed that robot manipulation tasks naturally divide into two phases: "contact-rich skills like grasping and placing" and "free-space motion over larger distances." While contact actions require the expressive power of a VLA to adapt based on visual feedback, moving through empty space does not require language understanding. In free space, classical motion planners (such as sampling-based planners) can solve geometric collision avoidance in milliseconds, making them vastly faster and safer.

The proposed method, "SkipVLA," leverages the frozen vision-language features of the VLA to predict target hover positions for planned motions. It offloads free-space transit to classical planners (such as VAMP or cuRoboV2) and queries the VLA only at the moments of grasping and placing. Task transitions are determined using gripper open/close states, requiring zero additional annotations or policy retraining.

Evaluations across simulation (13 LIBERO benchmark tasks) and real-world experiments (3 tasks on a physical 6-DoF YAM arm) using three different VLAs showed that task completion time was reduced by up to 2.5x (around a 60% reduction), and computational energy consumption on an NVIDIA Jetson Thor was cut by over 52%. Furthermore, because the classical planner resets error accumulation during transit, task success rates were maintained or even improved.
contributions: Proposed SkipVLA, a plug-and-play hybrid control framework that delegates free-space motion to classical planners and queries the VLA solely for contact-rich skills.
Developed a lightweight scoring head that reuses frozen vision-language tokens from the VLA to predict 3D target poses from existing imitation learning data without extra annotations.

Demonstrated up to a 2.5x speedup and over 52% energy savings while maintaining success rates across 13 simulation tasks, 3 real-world 6-DoF arm tasks, multiple VLAs (π0.5, SmolVLA, MolmoAct2), and different planners.

sections.heading: Why Run an Enormous AI for Every Single Motion?
sections.summary: While VLAs offer impressive generality, high inference latency creates a major bottleneck for practical deployment. This section introduces the concept and overview of SkipVLA, which splits manipulation tasks into contact actions and free-space motion, delegating transit to a classical planner.
sections.details:
Recent VLA models combine pretrained vision-language models with action generation heads, enabling robots to follow diverse natural language instructions and generalize to unseen environments. However, querying a multi-billion-parameter network every few actions introduces latency that vastly exceeds typical robot control cycles. In long-horizon tasks, this makes execution sluggish and consumes heavy computational resources.

Prior acceleration approaches include model distillation (compression), asynchronous action chunking (parallelizing inference and execution), and hierarchical architectures paired with smaller low-level policies. Yet, distillation often degrades performance, asynchrony introduces distribution shift risks from executing stale actions, and hierarchical setups require training specialized low-level policies from scratch. Most importantly, none of them solve the fundamental waste: calling a massive model even for simple movements through obstacle-free space.

Robot manipulation naturally decomposes into two parts: contact-rich, fine-grained skills (grasping, reorienting, placing) and coarse transit through free space (approaching objects, transporting them to a destination). Contact interactions require tight vision-action feedback loops, but free-space motion is purely a geometric collision-avoidance problem. Classical motion planners (sampling-based planners or trajectory optimization) can generate collision-free, safe trajectories in microseconds to milliseconds. However, classical planners lack semantic understanding and cannot determine "what to grasp" from language.

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces SkipVLA, a hybrid policy that uses the VLA's expressive representations to identify target poses, offloads free-space transit to a classical planner, and calls the VLA only for contact skills. It is a plug-and-play method that requires no extra data collection or VLA retraining.

captions.F1: The execution cycle of SkipVLA on a physical robot. From an initial pose, the planner moves the arm directly above the object (hover pose) (①). The VLA executes contact skills only during grasping (②). Once the gripper closes, the planner transports the arm above the box, and the VLA carries out the placing skill (③).

sections.heading: The Trajectory of Learning-Based Control and Classical Motion Planning
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work on VLA acceleration and integration with classical planners. Unlike methods relying purely on geometric optimization or restricting planners to recovery behaviors, SkipVLA cleanly divides roles using pretrained representations.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into three categories.

### VLA Models and Their Acceleration
Modern VLAs incorporating diffusion models or flow matching achieve remarkable expressiveness, but at high computational cost. Prior work has explored distilled models for lightweight execution, asynchronous chunking to mask latency, and hierarchical setups using smaller subtask policies. However, these methods consistently trade off out-of-distribution drift or the burden of retraining dedicated models.

### Strengths and Limits of Classical Motion Planning
Sampling-based motion planning (SBMP) and GPU-parallelized trajectory optimization (such as cuRobo) generate extremely fast trajectories with safety guarantees. However, operating strictly in coordinate geometry, they lack semantic reasoning and cannot autonomously deduce which object to target based on natural language.

### Integrating Foundation Models with Classical Planning
Other works have used foundation models to generate costmaps or relational constraints, solved via trajectory optimization (e.g., VoxPoser, ReKep). Yet, relying on geometric optimization for entire tasks struggles with complex, dynamic contact interactions that are hard to formulate as cost functions. Meanwhile, efforts integrating planners into learned policies (such as MPVI or LiLo-VLA) often restrict planners to recovering from out-of-distribution states or depend on predefined skill sequences.

In contrast, SkipVLA repurposes pretrained VLA vision-language features solely to select transit targets, dynamically bypassing free-space movement to classical planners during standard execution. It achieves dramatic latency reduction and collision avoidance without disrupting the VLA's learned policy.

captions.F2: Rollout and score evolution of SkipVLA on a LIBERO task. The bottom graph shows the predicted score probabilities for candidate target objects. As the arm reaches the hover pose via fast planner motion (blue), control switches to the VLA (orange). Once grasping completes, the next target (basket) is immediately selected, switching control back to planner transit.

sections.heading: The Math Behind VLA Control Cycles and Latency Bottlenecks
sections.summary: This section formalizes the VLA setup, action chunking, execution time breakdown, and imitation learning basics, pinning down why inference latency dominates control cycles.
sections.details:
Here, we outline the problem setup and notation.

Let $\pi^{\text{vla}}$ denote a generalist robot policy. This policy takes camera observations $\mathcal{O}_s$ (RGB-D workspace and wrist images), a natural language instruction $L$, and proprioceptive states $\mathbf{p}_s$ (joint angles and gripper states) as input, outputting robot actions at step $s$.

Modern VLAs typically do not output a single action per step. Instead, they use action chunking, predicting a sequence of $K$ future actions in a single forward pass. Queries to the model therefore occur every $K$ steps, within a set of query steps $\mathcal{Q}$.

The total execution time $\mathcal{T}(\tau)$ for a trajectory $\tau$ of length $N$ is expressed as:
$$\mathcal{T}(\tau) = N \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}} + |\mathcal{Q}| \Delta t_{\text{lat}}$$
where $\Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}$ is the robot's control period (the inverse of the sampling frequency) and $\Delta t_{\text{lat}}$ is the inference latency for computing an action chunk. In large VLAs, $\Delta t_{\text{lat}} \gg \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}$, making model query wait time the primary bottleneck preventing agile robot motions.

Additionally, standard imitation learning trains policies to minimize step-wise action loss over expert demonstration trajectories, which inherently penalizes deviations even when optimizing for faster, collision-free transit in free space.

sections.heading: How SkipVLA Works: Predicting the Goal, Skipping Transit, and Solving Only Contact
sections.summary: This section details SkipVLA's architecture, trajectory-level objective, target pose predictor, and self-supervised learning using gripper events. It requires no extra manual annotations by reusing existing demonstrations.
sections.details:
SkipVLA dynamically toggles between the VLA policy $\pi^{\text{vla}}$ and an ultra-low-latency classical control module $\pi^{\text{fast}}$ using an indicator module $I_s \in \{0, 1\}$.

### IV-A Problem Formulation and Trajectory-Level Objective
Classical planners generate geometrically and kinematically optimal collision-free trajectories. Forcing step-by-step imitation of human demonstrations penalizes these paths under standard loss functions, even if they are safe and faster. To address this, the authors introduce a trajectory-level objective that minimizes total execution time while ensuring the robot passes through critical key waypoints required for task success.

Specifically, trajectories are segmented into "contact manipulation segments" and "transit segments for approach and placement." The segment loss $\ell_{\text{seg}}$ requires strict step-by-step imitation during contact segments, but only requires matching start and end end-effector poses for transit segments.

### IV-B Implementation Details
The fast control module $\pi^{\text{fast}}$ consists of a target pose predictor $f_{\text{tgt}}$ and a low-level motion planner $\mathcal{P}$.
- **Target Pose Predictor ($f_{\text{tgt}}$)**: Candidate 3D object bounding boxes are extracted from observations using FastSAM and DBSCAN. Cross-attention is applied using frozen vision-language tokens from the VLA as Keys/Values and learnable positional embeddings for each box as Queries, followed by a lightweight MLP to score relevance. A collision-free hover pose directly above the highest-scoring box serves as the target pose $\mathbf{p}^{\text{tgt}}_s$.
- **Classical Planner ($\mathcal{P}$)**: Planners like VAMP or cuRoboV2 instantly generate trajectories from the current pose to the target pose.
- **Indicator Module ($I$)**: Transitions between skills rely on simple heuristics: whether the end-effector has reached the target hover pose (within tolerance $\epsilon_d$) and changes in gripper state (open to closed, or closed to open). Control transfers to the VLA upon approaching the target, and hands back to the planner once the gripper state changes.

### IV-C Training the Hybrid Setup
The VLA backbone remains completely frozen, and the planner requires no training. Thus, only the scoring head in the target pose predictor needs to be trained. In expert demonstrations, moments when the gripper state toggles (grasping or releasing) are detected, and the bounding box closest to the end-effector at that instant is automatically extracted as the ground truth. The scoring head is trained via cross-entropy loss, requiring zero manual annotations.

captions.F3: SkipVLA inference pipeline. Frozen VLA features are extracted from camera images and language instructions, then cross-attended with 3D bounding box candidates from point clouds to identify the target via scorer ($f_{\text{tgt}}$). The planner executes transit, and the VLA outputs actions only when the indicator ($I_s$) conditions are met.

sections.heading: Proven on Real Hardware and Simulation: Up to 2.5x Faster with Higher Success Rates
sections.summary: Validated in simulation across 13 LIBERO tasks and on a physical 6-DoF arm across 3 tasks. By drastically cutting inference queries, SkipVLA significantly reduced task duration, halved energy consumption, and boosted success rates by preventing error accumulation.
sections.details:
Experiments examined whether delegating transit to classical planners reduces time and query counts without harming task success rates, and whether the approach is robust across different planners and base VLAs.

### V-A Simulation Experiments (LIBERO)
SkipVLA was evaluated on LIBERO-Object (10 tasks) and LIBERO-10 (3 tasks) using the 3.5B-parameter "$\pi_{0.5}$" and the 0.5B-parameter "SmolVLA" as base models, with 50 trials per task.
Using VAMP as the planner, SkipVLA reduced execution time by 40% on LIBERO-Object and 27% on LIBERO-10. This reduction scaled proportionally with the drop in VLA queries, demonstrating the direct benefit of skipping unnecessary inferences. Replacing the planner with cuRoboV2 yielded similar gains, highlighting the framework's modularity.
Ablations replacing the indicator heuristic with object height changes showed stable performance, confirming design robustness.

### V-B Real-World Experiments (6-DoF YAM Arm)
On real hardware, $\pi_{0.5}$ and "MolmoAct2" served as backbones across three pick-and-place tasks of varying difficulty (single object, multi-object, and 3-block stacking) with 20 trials each. Computations and energy were benchmarked on an NVIDIA Jetson Thor.
- **Substantial Reductions in Execution Time and Query Count**: MolmoAct2 saw an average task completion time reduction of 46.0%, reaching up to 59.6% (a 2.47x speedup). $\pi_{0.5}$ achieved an average reduction of 30.6%. VLA inference queries dropped by 33.8% on average.
- **Energy Consumption Savings**: Per-trial energy use on Jetson Thor decreased by an average of 52.4% for MolmoAct2 and 29.1% for $\pi_{0.5}$, highlighting impressive energy efficiency for edge deployment.
- **The Welcome Bonus of Higher Success Rates**: Beyond faster execution, multi-object placement success rose from 90% to 100%, and precision block stacking improved by +15 percentage points on $\pi_{0.5}$ and +10 on MolmoAct2. In simulation with SmolVLA, success more than doubled from 39% to 82%.
This success boost occurs because SkipVLA curbs the compounding error typical of imitation learning (drift scaling as $O(\epsilon T^2)$ over horizon $T$). Classical planners transport the arm accurately and reset its position directly above the object before querying the VLA, effectively preventing the VLA from drifting out of distribution.

captions.F4: Comparison of elapsed time versus cumulative success rate across real-world tasks ((a) Single Object, (b) Multi-Object, (c) Block Stacking). For every task, SkipVLA (solid line) shifts significantly upward and to the left compared to baselines (dashed line), clearly reaching higher success rates in shorter amounts of time.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: SkipVLA cuts VLA inference calls by offloading free-space transit to classical planners, simultaneously achieving faster execution, lower energy use, and higher accuracy. It provides a practical solution requiring no model retraining.
sections.details:
This study presented SkipVLA, an approach that accelerates pretrained VLAs by delegating free-space motion to classical motion planners. By using a lightweight scorer over frozen VLA representations to set motion targets and calling the VLA only during contact phases, it achieved up to a 2.5x speedup and over 50% energy savings on real hardware.

Moreover, the classical planner serves as an anchor that resets error accumulation during transit, leading to task success rates equal to or higher than baselines. Requiring no large-scale retraining or additional data collection makes it highly attractive for real-world adoption.

Because the current implementation relies on gripper open/close events for task transitions, extending it to non-pick-and-place contact tasks (such as wiping or opening doors) remains a challenge. Future work will explore learned temporal segmentation to generalize across all types of manipulation tasks.

takeaways: End-to-end VLA execution across an entire manipulation task is unnecessary; a hybrid setup dividing coarse transit from delicate contact is far more effective.
Interleaving classical planning does more than speed up motion; it physically cuts off compounding errors, resetting the out-of-distribution drift that plagues imitation learning.
Pretrained representations in large VLAs can be efficiently repurposed for goal-prediction tasks like bounding box matching without requiring extra demonstration annotations.
limitations: Because the current transition indicator relies on gripper open/close events, it cannot be applied directly to continuous contact tasks that do not involve grasping or placing (such as wiping or tool use).
The approach assumes top-down grasps for 3D bounding box prediction and hover pose generation, requiring extensions to handle side approaches or complex 6-DoF grasp poses.

It relies on off-the-shelf segmentation tools like FastSAM and DBSCAN for object detection, limiting robustness in environments with severe occlusion, transparent objects, or deformable items where detectors struggle.
